title: Part 2, Chapter 32
paragraphs: About the reply Don Quixote gave his critic, with other incidents grave and droll

Don Quixote, then, having risen to his feet, trembling from head to foot like a man dosed with mercury, said in a hurried, agitated voice, "The place I am in, the presence I stand in, and the respect I have always had for the profession to which your worship belongs, hold and bind the hands of my just indignation. For these reasons, and because I know, as everyone knows, that a clergyman's weapon is the same as a woman's — the tongue — I will with mine engage in equal combat with your worship, from whom one might have expected good advice instead of foul abuse. Pious, well-meant reproof requires a different bearing and arguments of another sort; in any case, to have reproved me in public, and so roughly, oversteps the bounds of proper reproof — that comes better with gentleness than with rudeness. And it isn't fitting to call the sinner an outright blockhead and fool, without knowing anything about the sin being reproved. Come, tell me — for which of the stupidities you have observed in me do you condemn and abuse me, and order me home to look after my house and wife and children, without knowing whether I have any? Is nothing more needed than to wangle one's way into other people's houses to rule over the masters — and that, perhaps, after having been brought up in all the narrowness of some seminary, without ever having seen more of the world than may lie within twenty or thirty leagues around — to be fit to lay down the law rashly for chivalry, and pass judgment on knights-errant? Is it perhaps an idle occupation, or is the time ill-spent that is spent in roaming the world in quest, not of its pleasures, but of those arduous toils by which the good rise upwards to the abodes of everlasting life? If gentlemen, great lords, nobles, men of high birth, were to rate me a fool, I should take it as an irreparable insult; but I don't care a farthing if clerics who have never entered upon or trod the paths of chivalry should think me foolish. A knight I am, and a knight I will die, if it pleases the Most High. Some take the broad road of overweening ambition; others that of mean and servile flattery; others that of deceitful hypocrisy, and some that of true religion. But I, guided by my star, follow the narrow path of knight-errantry, and in pursuit of that calling I despise wealth, but not honour. I have redressed injuries, righted wrongs, punished insolences, defeated giants, and crushed monsters. I am in love, for no other reason than that knights-errant are required to be so; but though I am, I am no carnal-minded lover — I am one of the chaste, platonic sort. My intentions are always directed to worthy ends: to do good to all and evil to none. And if a man who means this, does this, and makes this his practice deserves to be called a fool, then it is for your highnesses to say, most excellent duke and duchess."

"Good, by God!" cried Sancho. "Say no more in your own defence, master mine, because there's nothing more in the world to be said, thought, or insisted on. And besides — when this gentleman denies, as he has, that there are or ever have been knights-errant in the world, is it any wonder if he knows nothing of what he's been talking about?"
"Are you, perhaps, brother," said the ecclesiastic, "that Sancho Panza they mention, the one to whom your master has promised an island?"

"Yes, I am," said Sancho, "and what's more, I'm one who deserves it as much as anyone. I'm one of the sort — 'Attach yourself to the good, and you'll be one of them,' and of those who 'Not with whom you're bred, but with whom you're fed,' and of those who 'Lean against a good tree, and good shade covers them.' I've leant on a good master, and I've been going about with him for months, and please God I'll turn out to be just like him; long life to him and long life to me, because he won't be short of empires to rule, or I of islands to govern."
"No, friend Sancho, certainly not," said the duke. "In the name of Señor Don Quixote, I confer on you the government of one — not a small one either — that I have at my disposal."
"Down on your knees, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and kiss the feet of his excellency for the favour he has granted you."

Sancho obeyed, and on seeing this the ecclesiastic stood up from the table completely out of temper, exclaiming, "By the gown I wear, I'm almost ready to say that your excellency is as big a fool as these sinners. No wonder they're mad, when people in their senses sanction their madness! I leave your excellency to them, because as long as they are in the house, I will stay in my own and spare myself the trouble of reproving what I cannot remedy." And without uttering another word or eating another bite, he stalked off, the entreaties of the duke and duchess being entirely useless to stop him — not that the duke said much to him, because he couldn't, on account of the laughter the man's uncalled-for anger provoked.

When he had stopped laughing, he said to Don Quixote, "You have replied on your own behalf so stoutly, Sir Knight of the Lions, that there's no need to seek further satisfaction for this, which, though it may look like an offence, is not so at all — because, as women can give no offence, no more can ecclesiastics, as you very well know."

"That is true," said Don Quixote, "and the reason is that he who is not liable to offence cannot give offence to anyone. Women, children, and ecclesiastics, since they cannot defend themselves, though they may receive offence cannot be insulted — because between the offence and the insult there is, as your excellency very well knows, this difference: the insult comes from someone capable of offering it, who does so, and maintains it; the offence may come from any quarter without carrying insult with it. To take an example: a man is standing unsuspectingly in the street, and ten others come up armed and beat him; he draws his sword and conducts himself like a man, but the number of his opponents makes it impossible for him to achieve his purpose and avenge himself; this man suffers an offence but not an insult. Another example will make the same thing plain: a man is standing with his back turned, another comes up and strikes him, and after striking him takes to flight without waiting an instant, and the first man pursues him but does not overtake him; the one who received the blow received an offence, but not an insult, because an insult must be maintained. If the man who struck him, even though he did so sneakingly and treacherously, had drawn his sword and stood and faced him, then the one who was struck would have received offence and insult at the same time — offence because he was struck treacherously, insult because the striker maintained what he had done, standing his ground without running away. And so, according to the laws of the accursed duel, I may have received offence, but not insult, since neither women nor children can maintain it, nor can they wound, nor have they any way of standing their ground — and it's just the same with those who belong to religion. These three sorts of persons are without arms offensive or defensive, and so, although by nature they are bound to defend themselves, they have no right to offend anybody. And although I said just now that I might have received offence, I now say certainly not, because he who cannot receive an insult can still less give one. For these reasons I ought not to feel, nor do I feel, aggrieved at what that good man said to me. I only wish he had stayed a little longer, so I might have shown him the mistake he makes in supposing and maintaining that there are not and never have been any knights-errant in the world; if Amadis or any of his countless descendants had heard him say as much, I am sure it would not have gone well with his worship."

"I'll take my oath of that," said Sancho. "They would have given him a slash that would have split him from top to toe like a pomegranate or a ripe melon; they were just the fellows to put up with jokes of that sort! By my faith, I'm certain if Reinaldos of Montalban had heard the little man's words, he'd have given him such a smack on the mouth that he wouldn't have spoken for the next three years. Let him tackle them, and he'll see how he gets out of their hands!"
The duchess, listening to Sancho, was ready to die laughing, and in her own mind she set him down as droller and madder than his master; and there were quite a few just then who shared that opinion.

Don Quixote finally calmed down, and dinner came to an end, and as the tablecloth was being cleared, four damsels came in: one with a silver basin, another with a jug also of silver, a third with two fine white towels over her shoulder, and the fourth with her arms bared to the elbows and in her white hands (white they certainly were) a round ball of Naples soap. The one with the basin approached, and with arch composure and impudence thrust it under Don Quixote's chin. Wondering at such a ceremony, he said never a word, supposing it was the custom of that country to wash beards instead of hands. So he stretched his out as far as he could, and at that instant the jug began to pour and the damsel with the soap rubbed his beard briskly, raising snowflakes — for the soap lather was no less white — not only over his beard but all over his face, even over the eyes of the submissive knight, so that he was forced to keep them shut. The duke and duchess, who had known nothing about this, waited to see how the strange washing would end. The barber-damsel, when she had him a hand's breadth deep in lather, pretended there was no more water, and told the one with the jug to go and fetch some, while Señor Don Quixote waited. She did so, and Don Quixote was left the strangest and most ridiculous figure imaginable. Everyone present — and there were quite a few — was watching him, and as they saw him there with half a yard of neck on display, uncommonly brown, his eyes shut, and his beard full of soap, it was a great wonder, and only by enormous self-discipline, that they were able to keep from laughing. The damsels, the engineers of the joke, kept their eyes down, not daring to look at their master and mistress; and as for the duke and duchess, laughter and anger struggled within them, and they didn't know what to do — whether to punish the audacity of the girls or to reward them for the amusement they had had from seeing Don Quixote in such a state.

At length the damsel with the jug returned and they finished washing Don Quixote, and the one carrying the towels very deliberately wiped him and dried him; and all four together, making him a profound bow and curtsy, were about to leave when the duke, lest Don Quixote see through the joke, called out to the one with the basin, saying, "Come and wash me, and make sure there's water enough." The girl, sharp-witted and quick, came and placed the basin for the duke just as she had for Don Quixote, and they soon had him well soaped and washed, and after wiping him dry they made their bow and withdrew. It came out afterwards that the duke had sworn that if they had not washed him as they had Don Quixote, he would have punished them for their impudence — which they cleverly atoned for by soaping him as well.

Sancho watched the washing ceremony very attentively and said to himself, "God bless me, if only it were the custom in this country to wash squires' beards too as well as knights'. Because by God and on my soul, I want it badly; and if they gave me a scrape of the razor besides, I'd take it as an even greater kindness."
"What are you saying to yourself, Sancho?" asked the duchess.

"I was saying, señora," he replied, "that in the courts of other princes, I've always heard that when the cloth is taken away, they give water for the hands, but not lye for the beard; and that shows it's good to live long so you can see a lot. To be sure they say too that whoever lives a long life must endure a lot of evil, though to endure a washing of that sort is pleasure rather than pain."
"Don't be uneasy, friend Sancho," said the duchess. "I'll see to it that my damsels wash you, and even put you in the tub if necessary."
"I'll settle for the beard," said Sancho, "at least for now; and as for the future, God has decided what will be."
"Attend to worthy Sancho's request, seneschal," said the duchess, "and do exactly what he wishes."

The seneschal replied that Señor Sancho would be obeyed in everything; and with that he went off to dinner and took Sancho along with him, while the duke and duchess and Don Quixote remained at the table discussing a great variety of things, all bearing on the calling of arms and knight-errantry.

The duchess begged Don Quixote, since he seemed to have a sharp memory, to describe and portray for her the beauty and features of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, because, judging by what rumour trumpeted abroad of her beauty, she felt sure Dulcinea must be the fairest creature in the world, indeed in all La Mancha.

Don Quixote sighed on hearing the duchess's request, and said, "If I could pluck out my heart and lay it on a plate on this table here before your highness's eyes, it would spare my tongue the pain of telling what can hardly be thought, for in it your excellency would see her portrayed in full. But why should I attempt to depict and describe in detail, feature by feature, the beauty of the peerless Dulcinea — a burden worthy of other shoulders than mine, an enterprise in which the brushes of Parrhasius, Timantes, and Apelles, and the chisel of Lysippus ought to be employed, to paint it in pictures and carve it in marble and bronze, and Ciceronian and Demosthenian eloquence to sound its praises?"
"What does Demosthenian mean, Señor Don Quixote?" said the duchess. "It's a word I never heard in all my life."
"Demosthenian eloquence," said Don Quixote, "means the eloquence of Demosthenes, as Ciceronian means that of Cicero, who were the two most eloquent orators in the world."

"True," said the duke; "you must have lost your wits to ask such a question. Nevertheless, Señor Don Quixote would greatly gratify us if he would depict her for us; never fear, even in an outline or sketch she'll be something to make the fairest envious."

"I would do so, certainly," said Don Quixote, "had she not been blurred to my mind's eye by the misfortune that fell upon her a short time ago — one of such a nature that I am more ready to weep over it than to describe it. Your highnesses must know that, going a few days back to kiss her hands and receive her blessing, approval, and permission for this third sally, I found her altogether a different being from the one I sought. I found her enchanted and changed from a princess into a peasant, from fair to foul, from an angel into a devil, from fragrant to foul-smelling, from refined to clownish, from a dignified lady into a leaping tomboy — in a word, from Dulcinea del Toboso into a coarse Sayago wench."

"God bless me!" cried the duke aloud at this. "Who can have done the world such an injury? Who can have robbed it of the beauty that gladdened it, of the grace and gaiety that charmed it, of the modesty that gave it lustre?"

"Who?" replied Don Quixote. "Who could it be but some malignant enchanter, one of the many who persecute me out of envy — that accursed race born into the world to obscure and bring to nothing the achievements of the good, and to glorify and exalt the deeds of the wicked? Enchanters have persecuted me, enchanters persecute me still, and enchanters will continue to persecute me until they have sunk me and my lofty chivalry in the deep abyss of oblivion; and they injure and wound me where they know I feel it most. Because to deprive a knight-errant of his lady is to deprive him of the eyes he sees with, of the sun that gives him light, of the food by which he lives. I've said it many times before, and I say it once more now: a knight-errant without a lady is like a tree without leaves, a building without a foundation, or a shadow without the body that casts it."

"There's no denying it," said the duchess. "But still, if we are to believe the history of Don Quixote that has come out here lately to general applause, it is to be inferred from it, if I'm not mistaken, that you never saw the lady Dulcinea, and that she is nothing in the world but an imaginary lady — one you yourself begot and gave birth to in your brain, and adorned with whatever charms and perfections you chose."

"There's a good deal to be said on that point," said Don Quixote. "God knows whether there is a Dulcinea in the world or not, or whether she is imaginary or not imaginary; these are matters whose proof must not be pushed to extreme lengths. I have not begotten nor given birth to my lady, though I see her as she has to be — a lady who contains in herself all the qualities that would make her famous throughout the world: beautiful without blemish, dignified without haughtiness, tender and yet modest, gracious from courtesy and courteous from good breeding, and finally, of exalted lineage, because beauty shines forth and excels with a higher degree of perfection in those of good blood than in the fair of low birth."

"That is true," said the duke. "But Señor Don Quixote will give me leave to say what I am compelled to say by the story of his exploits that I've read, from which one infers that, granting there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, or out of it, and that she is in the highest degree beautiful as you have described her to us, as for the loftiness of her lineage she is not on a par with the Orianas, Alastrajareas, Madasimas, or others of that sort, with whom, as you well know, the histories abound."

"To that I may reply," said Don Quixote, "that Dulcinea is the daughter of her own deeds, that virtues rectify blood, and that lowly virtue is more to be regarded and esteemed than exalted vice. Besides, Dulcinea has something in her that may raise her to be a crowned and sceptred queen — because the merit of a fair and virtuous woman is capable of performing greater miracles than that. And though not formally, she virtually has higher fortunes within herself."

"I declare, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that in everything you say, you proceed most cautiously and with the bridle in hand, as the saying goes. From now on I'll believe in her myself, and I'll see to it that everyone in my house believes — even my lord the duke if necessary — that there is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, that she is alive today, that she is beautiful and nobly born and deserves to have such a knight as Señor Don Quixote in her service, which is the highest praise I have it in my power to give her, or that I can think of. But I can't help having a small doubt, and a certain grudge against Sancho Panza. The doubt is this: the aforesaid history declares that the said Sancho Panza, when he carried a letter on your worship's behalf to the said lady Dulcinea, found her sifting a sack of wheat; and what's more, it says it was red wheat — a thing which makes me doubt the loftiness of her lineage."

To this Don Quixote made answer, "Señora, your highness must know that everything, or almost everything, that happens to me transcends the ordinary limits of what happens to other knights-errant, whether it's directed by the inscrutable will of destiny, or by the malice of some jealous enchanter. Now it's an established fact that all or most famous knights-errant have some special gift — one is invulnerable to enchantment, another is made of such impenetrable flesh that he cannot be wounded, like the famous Roland, one of the twelve peers of France, of whom it's said he could not be wounded except in the sole of his left foot, and only with the point of a stout pin and no other sort of weapon. And so, when Bernardo del Carpio slew him at Roncesvalles, finding that he couldn't wound him with steel, he lifted him up from the ground in his arms and strangled him, calling to mind in good time the death Hercules inflicted on Antaeus, the fierce giant said to be the son of Terra. I would infer from what I've mentioned that perhaps I may have some gift of this kind — not that of being invulnerable, because experience has proved to me many times that I am of tender flesh and not at all impenetrable; nor that of being proof against enchantment, because I've already seen myself thrust into a cage in which all the world would not have been able to confine me except by force of enchantments. But since I delivered myself from that one, I'm inclined to believe there's no other that can harm me. And so, these enchanters, seeing they can't exert their vile craft against my person, take revenge on what I love most, and try to rob me of life by maltreating that of Dulcinea, in whom I live. And therefore I am convinced that when my squire carried my message to her, they changed her into a common peasant girl, engaged in such a mean occupation as sifting wheat; but as I have already said, that wheat was not red wheat, nor wheat at all, but grains of oriental pearl. And as a proof of all this, I must tell your highnesses that, coming to El Toboso a short time ago, I was altogether unable to find the palace of Dulcinea; and the next day, though Sancho my squire saw her in her own proper shape, which is the fairest in the world, to me she appeared to be a coarse, ill-favoured farm-girl, by no means well-spoken either — she who is propriety itself. And so, since I am not and, so far as one can judge, cannot be enchanted, it is she who is enchanted, blighted, altered, changed, transformed; in her my enemies have taken their revenge on me, and for her shall I live in ceaseless tears until I see her restored to her original state. I have mentioned this so that nobody should mind what Sancho said about Dulcinea's winnowing or sifting; for as they changed her to me, it's no wonder if they changed her to him. Dulcinea is illustrious and well-born, and of one of the noble families of El Toboso, which are many, ancient, and good. In which, most assuredly, the share of the peerless Dulcinea is no small one, through whom her town will be famous and celebrated in ages to come, as Troy was through Helen, and Spain through La Cava — though with a better title and tradition. For another thing: I would have your graces understand that Sancho Panza is one of the drollest squires that ever served a knight-errant. Sometimes there is a sharpness about his simplicity that it's an amusement to try and work out whether he is simple or sharp. He has mischievous tricks that stamp him a rogue, and blundering ways that prove him a fool. He doubts everything and believes everything; when I think he's about to come down headlong from sheer stupidity, he comes out with something so shrewd it sends him up to the skies. After all, I would not exchange him for another squire, even if I were given a city to boot, and that's why I am in doubt whether it will be a good idea to send him to the government your highness has bestowed on him. Although I perceive in him a certain aptitude for the work of governing — so that, with a little trimming of his understanding, he would manage any government as easily as the king does his taxes; and besides, we already have ample experience that it doesn't require much cleverness or much learning to be a governor, because there are a hundred around us who scarcely know how to read and yet govern like gerfalcons. The main point is that they should have good intentions and be desirous of doing right in all things, because they'll never lack for people to advise and direct them in what they have to do, like those knight-governors who, being no lawyers, pronounce sentences with the aid of an assessor. My advice to him will be to take no bribe and surrender no right, and I have some other little matters in reserve, which will come out in due season for Sancho's benefit and the advantage of the island he is to govern."

The duke, duchess, and Don Quixote had reached this point in their conversation when they heard voices and a great hubbub in the palace, and Sancho burst abruptly into the room, glowing with anger, with a straining-cloth tied around him by way of a bib, and followed by several servants — or more properly speaking, kitchen-boys and other underlings — one of whom carried a small trough full of water that from its colour and impurity was plainly dishwater. The one with the trough pursued him everywhere he went, trying with the utmost persistence to thrust it under his chin, while another kitchen-boy seemed bent on washing his beard.
"What is all this, brothers?" asked the duchess. "What is it? What do you want to do to this good man? Do you forget he is a governor-elect?"
To which the barber kitchen-boy replied, "The gentleman will not let himself be washed as is customary, and as my lord and the señor his master have been."

"Yes I will," said Sancho, in a great rage, "but I'd like it to be with cleaner towels, clearer lye, and not such dirty hands. There's not so much difference between me and my master that he should be washed with angels' water and I with devil's lye. The customs of countries and princes' palaces are only good as long as they cause no annoyance, but the way of washing they have here is worse than doing penance. I have a clean beard, and I don't need to be freshened up in that fashion, and whoever comes to wash me or touch a hair of my head — I mean to say my beard, with all due respect — I'll give him a punch that will leave my fist sunk in his skull. These ceremonies and soapings are more like jokes than the polite attentions of one's host."

The duchess was ready to die with laughter when she saw Sancho's rage and heard his words; but it was no pleasure to Don Quixote to see him in such a sorry state, with the dingy towel about him and the hangers-on of the kitchen all around him. So, making a low bow to the duke and duchess as if to ask their permission to speak, he addressed the rabble in a dignified tone: "Here now, gentlemen! Leave that young man alone, and go back where you came from, or anywhere else if you like. My squire is as clean as anyone, and those troughs are no more proper for him than narrow, thin-necked jars. Take my advice and leave him be, because neither he nor I understand joking."

Sancho took the word out of his mouth and went on, "No, let them come and try their jokes on the country bumpkin — it's about as likely I'll stand for it as that it's now midnight! Let them bring me a comb here, or whatever they please, and curry this beard of mine, and if they get anything out of it that offends against cleanliness, let them clip me to the skin."

At this the duchess, laughing all the while, said, "Sancho Panza is right, and always will be in everything he says. He is clean, and as he says himself, he doesn't need to be washed; and if our ways don't please him, he's free to choose. Besides, you promoters of cleanliness have been excessively careless and thoughtless — I don't know whether I shouldn't say audacious — to bring troughs and wooden utensils and kitchen dishcloths, instead of basins and jugs of pure gold and towels of Holland linen, to such a person and such a beard. But after all, you're ill-bred and ill-conditioned, and spiteful as you are, you can't help showing the grudge you bear the squires of knights-errant."

The impudent servants, and even the seneschal who came with them, took the duchess to be speaking in earnest, so they removed the straining-cloth from Sancho's neck, and with something like shame and confusion in their faces, they all went off and left him. Whereupon Sancho, seeing himself safe out of what to him had seemed the most extreme danger, ran and fell on his knees before the duchess, saying, "From great ladies, great favours may be looked for. The favour your grace has done me today cannot be repaid with anything less than wishing I were dubbed a knight-errant, to devote myself all the days of my life to the service of so exalted a lady. I am a labouring man, my name is Sancho Panza, I am married, I have children, and I'm serving as a squire. If in any one of these capacities I can serve your highness, I won't be longer in obeying than your grace is in commanding."

"It's easy to see, Sancho," replied the duchess, "that you've learned to be polite in the school of politeness itself; I mean to say it's easy to see that you have been nursed in the bosom of Señor Don Quixote, who is, of course, the cream of good breeding and flower of ceremony — or cirimony, as you'd say yourself. Fair be the fortunes of such a master and such a servant — the one the polestar of knight-errantry, the other the star of squirely fidelity! Rise, Sancho my friend; I'll repay your courtesy by seeing to it that my lord the duke makes good on the promised gift of the government as soon as possible."

With this the conversation came to an end, and Don Quixote went off to take his midday nap; but the duchess begged Sancho, unless he had a strong desire to sleep, to come and spend the afternoon with her and her damsels in a very cool chamber. Sancho replied that, though he certainly had the habit of sleeping four or five hours in the heat of the day in summer, to serve her excellency he would try with all his might not to sleep even one that day, and that he would come in obedience to her command. And with that he went off. The duke gave fresh orders for treating Don Quixote as a knight-errant, without departing even in the smallest particular from the style in which, as the stories tell us, they used to treat the knights of old.
